https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_wa.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania warns of Mere attempts to bypass EU sanctions via rebranding 2026-07-28 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania's Economy and Innovation Ministry has warned of possible attempts to circumvent European Union sanctions following the sudden closure of Mere retail stores, which are linked to Russia's Svetofor Group. Deputy Minister Paulius Petrauskas said on Monday that the group may be attempting to bypass restrictions by rebranding. The ministry suspects that Mere stores could be renamed Ola. The ministry has asked the Financial Crime Investigation Service to assess whether individuals sanctioned under the European Union's 21st sanctions package are connected to companies or other entities operating in Lithuania and whether there are grounds to impose restrictive measures against them. "When sanctioned Russian business interests attempt to re-enter our market under different names or through intermediaries, it is not just a business matter - it is an attempt to circumvent European Union sanctions," Minister Edvinas Griksas said. Last week, the European Union announced sanctions against an additional 168 entities and 48 individuals, including the owners of Svetofor Group, which operates the Mere retail chain. Russian businessman Sergey Shnayder, the owner of Mere, has been added to the sanctions list. Reports of Mere store closures in Lithuania emerged last week. At the time, the company said all stores had been closed due to "technical obstacles" but declined to comment on whether the closures were temporary or related to sanctions. As of Monday, the Mere website was offline and the company's Facebook account had been deleted. Svetofor Group founders and co-owners operate more than 2,200 stores in Russia and other countries under the Svetofor, Mere and MyPrice brands. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Police have charged three teenage Scots College students after a 14-year-old girl was last week allegedly assaulted in an alleyway in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. Photograph: Paul Miller/AAP View image in fullscreen Police have charged three teenage Scots College students after a 14-year-old girl was last week allegedly assaulted in an alleyway in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. Photograph: Paul Miller/AAP New South Wales Three private school students charged after alleged sexual assault of 14-year-old girl in Sydney’s east The three teenagers are students at Scots College, one of Sydney’s oldest boys’ private schools Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.49 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three students from a Sydney boys’ private school have been charged with sexual assault offences in relation to the alleged assault of a teenage girl. Police launched an investigation after reports that a 14-year-old girl had last month been assaulted in an alleyway in Sydney’s eastern suburbs. On Thursday morning, authorities conducted search warrants at several homes, where a number of electronic devices were seized and are awaiting forensic examination. During the searches, police also found two replica firearms, a Glock-style BB gun, three laser pointers and a number plate believed to have been stolen. All three boys were arrested and taken into custody. Two boys were charged with two counts of aggravated sexual assault in company with others and aggravated sexual touching of another person. The other boy was charged with one count of the same offences, police said. All three teenagers have been released on bail under strict conditions and are expected to appear before a children’s court later this month. The three boys are students at The Scots College, one of Sydney’s oldest and most expensive boys’ schools, where fees cost up to $47,000 a year. In a statement, the school said it was aware of the “alleged incident that occurred outside school hours” and is cooperating with police. “The College takes this matter seriously and has cooperated … we believe it is important that the police investigation is allowed to take its course and it would not be appropriate for the College to comment further on the matter”, the statement read. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62j.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Putin warned that "if anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth" By Steve Rosenberg Russia editor, Moscow Published 8 hours ago Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine. "That's a secret. A military secret." Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging. And that, I suspect, is the point. Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine. It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares". Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like. We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK. But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe. Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport. Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe". Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK? Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference. So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks. "If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks." Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine. The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind. For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine. Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure. "I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on. Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war". "War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference. He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys. "We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them." There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip. Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon? There's nothing in the diary. Not yet. But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP View image in fullscreen Emergency workers clear debris and damaged road infrastructure near a destroyed car after a Russian overnight strike in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky Zelenskyy says ballistic missiles hit crowded areas with no military facilities nearby; truce comes amid reports of growing humanitarian crisis. What we know on day 1,707 Guardian staff and agencies Mon 26 Oct 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded eight , with mayor Vitali Klitschko saying medical facilities and an intensive care unit had been damaged in the late Monday attack. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a ballistic missile attack had struck the grounds of a university campus in the Ukrainian capital. “The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure,” he said on social media. The strikes on Kyiv came hours before a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was due to start , after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages . The truce, aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into Oleshky, was to begin at 3am local time (0100 GMT). No end date for the truce has been provided. The city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in the crosshairs of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces. Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the US has said who would monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it. The Russian defence ministry said on Friday it would halt fire in the “Kherson sector” for the duration of the ceasefire. Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow has denied. Before the latest strikes on Kyiv, Zelenskyy highlighted ​Ukraine was still waiting for US defence secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on critical missile supplies . “We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I instructed our team to raise this with the ⁠American side once again,” he said on X. Romania said on Monday that a network “coordinated” from Russia was involved in starting a fire near an arms factory . The fire broke out on 14 September near an arms factory in the central city of Brasov and two Belarusians and a Ukrainian – residents in EU countries – were involved, authorities said. Two of them were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offences”, the office for organised crime said. The third is at large in Poland, it added. Russia’s embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment but Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations. The attack in Brasov is the latest in a string of similar incidents in Europe , with Nato and the EU grappling with what they say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference by the Kremlin aimed at undercutting Western support for Kyiv. Over the past three weeks, at ​least eight cargo ​ships have been hit off the coast of Nato members Romania and Bulgaria. Some 34 sailors are reported dead or missing. Ukraine’s military has begun using specialised aerial rescue drones to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield , carrying two stranded troops to safety near the Russian border in the first such operations. The newly developed StarGate drone, a six-rotor aircraft fitted with an enclosed evacuation capsule, was used in two separate missions over the past week, the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, an elite unit, said on Monday. Developed by Ukrainian technology company SkyFall, the drone is intended to reduce rescue times from hours to minutes, reaching hard-to-access combat zones currently served by unmanned ground vehicles.
